claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations with a thermal ramp can be used to study the size-dependent thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will have lower melting temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will have lower thermal stability than larger nanoparticles.
The reduced thermal stability of smaller nanoparticles is caused by enhanced surface effects.
The FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a uniform composition across the investigated sizes.
Nanoparticle size determines the surface-to-volume ratio.
At elevated temperatures, surface diffusion is enhanced in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface diffusion accelerates atomic rearrangements in smaller nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface diffusion accelerates defect formation in smaller nanoparticles.
Accelerated atomic rearrangement and defect formation cause melting to begin earlier in smaller nanoparticles.
Accelerated atomic rearrangement and defect formation cause phase transitions to occur earlier in smaller nanoparticles.
Larger nanoparticles or bulk FeCuCrCoNi systems maintain higher melting temperatures than smaller nanoparticles.
Larger nanoparticles or bulk FeCuCrCoNi systems maintain greater thermal stability than smaller nanoparticles.
Excluding substrates and reactive species prevents environmental interactions from affecting the simulated thermal response.
The predicted thermal response depends on the accuracy of the molecular-dynamics interatomic potential used for the HEA.
Simulation parameters and interatomic-potential fidelity can change predicted transition temperatures and kinetic details.
A change in potential energy can be used to identify melting in the simulations.
